There are still some legitimate uses of parts of the Imperial system of measurement, e.g.:

As I learned in my first semester engineering class in college, the pound (lb) is actually a far more versatile unit than the kilogram, since the default measurement of a pound is pounds force (lbf).

One pound-force is defined as the force required to accelerate a mass of one slug (32.174 lbm) at a rate of 1 foot/second2. To get pounds-mass from pounds-force, you divide pounds-force by the gravitational constant of whatever astral body (planet, star, moon, etc.) you're on.

Here on earth, the gravitational constant is 32.174 feet/second2 (note the similarity to the mass of one slug), so one pound-force is equivalent to one pound-mass. On Jupiter, where gravity is much stronger, one pound-force is much less than one pound-mass, and on the moon, one pound-force is greater than one pound-mass.

Obviously, to get pounds-force from pounds-mass, you just multiply by the gravitational constant instead of dividing.

This system allows you to measure the mass of an object here on earth, and you can easily calculate the pounds force that will be exerted on parts of that object by different gravitational pulls, whereas in Metric, there is no simple conversion from mass to force.
